svg.title: Figure GK-5. Hours-of-service timeline (property-carrying)
svg.desc: Federal 11-hour / 14-hour and California 12-hour / 16-hour figures from CA Commercial Driver Handbook DL 650 (REV 12/2019) Hours of Service discussion (Section 2) and 49 CFR 395. Confirm current FMCSR and California hours-of-service rules before you dispatch; they are updated periodically.

svg.text: Two different clocks: interstate (federal FMCSR) vs. California intrastate. Do not mix them. Passenger-carrier rules are omitted here.

text.font-family: Liberation Sans, DejaVu Sans, Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif

svg.text: Federal (interstate) -- after 10 consecutive hours off duty

text.tspan: You may drive up to 11 hours, but not after the 14th hour after coming on duty following 10 hours off. You may do other
work after the 14th hour, but you may not drive. Weekly 60/70-hour limits and sleeper-berth rules are in 49 CFR 395 (the
30-minute break rule is federal; it is not in the DL 650 HOS table).

svg.text: California intrastate -- after 10 consecutive hours off duty

text.tspan: In California intrastate commerce you may drive up to 12 hours, but not after the 16th hour after coming on duty
(handbook Hours of Service table). Use California rules only when you are truly operating intrastate under those rules.

text.font-family: Liberation Sans, DejaVu Sans, Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif
text.tspan: On duty includes driving and other work (loading, inspections, waiting to be dispatched when required to be ready, etc.). Off duty is not on-duty time.
Falsifying a log is a serious violation. Keep a current graph-grid log or the ELD record your operation uses, plus supporting documents.
Adverse driving / exception provisions are narrow -- do not assume you can just finish the trip. When tired, stop, even if hours remain.
This chart is a memory aid for the knowledge test and safe scheduling. Always follow the rule set that applies to that trip (federal vs. CA, cargo vs. passenger, ELD exemptions).
